# Relationship between AI / ML / Deep Learning

## Hierarchy

```
인공지능 (AI)
 └─ 머신러닝 (Machine Learning)
      └─ 딥러닝 (Deep Learning)  ← 이 강의의 주제
```

According to Fig. 1.4 of the Goodfellow textbook, deep learning is a type of **Representation Learning** 
, representation learning is a type of machine learning, and machine learning is one of several methods of approaching AI 
. Non-ML methods, such as knowledge base systems, are also included in AI.

## Core Ideas of Machine Learning

Structural Differences Between Traditional Programming and Machine Learning:

| Paradigm | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|
| **Traditional Programming** | Data + Program | Output |
| **Machine Learning** | Data + Output(Label) | **Program**(Model) |

Mathematically, 
it is to find a function $f$ that predicts $y^*$ for an unknown input $x^*$ from the data pair $\{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i=1}^N$.

$$f: \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}$$

## Two classification axes of ML problems

$$\text{Classification of ML problems} \neq \text{Categorization of ML problems}$$

Both terms are translated as "classification" and may be confusing, but **the reference axes are different**.

### Classification of ML problems — Based on output type

This is a classification based on the question "What does the model predict?"

| Task | Output | Main Learning Method |
|---|---|---|
| **Classification** | Discrete Label $y \in \{1,\ldots,K\}$ | Usually supervised |
| **Regression** | Continuous value $y \in \mathbb{R}$ | Usually supervised |
| **Similarity** | Similar/Dissimilar Pairs | Usually supervised |
| **Clustering** | Cluster Structure | Usually unsupervised |
| **Embedding** | Vector $z \in \mathbb{R}^d$ | Usually unsupervised |
| **Reinforcement Learning** | Behavior Policy $\pi$ | RL |

### Categorization of ML problems — Based on learning method

This is a classification based on the question "How does the model learn?"

| Method | Label Usage | Features |
|---|---|---|
| **Supervised** | Use All | Accurate, High Label Cost |
| **Unsupervised** | None | Cheap, structure found |
| **Semi-supervised** | Partial use | Practical compromise |
| **Active learning** | Optional use | Efficient labeling |
| **Reinforcement** | Indirect Use | Agent Behavior Optimization |

::: {.callout-important}
## Key distinction

The two classifications are **two independent axes**. Even for the same Classification task, 
training can be performed using supervised, unsupervised, or semi-supervised methods. 
Additionally, in "Classification of ML problems," "Classification" 
refers to a meta-level classification behavior, and since one of the results is the "Classification task," 
there is a circular structure that appears to be a tautology.
:::

# Key Concepts: Embedding, Manifold, Latent Space, Epoch

These are the four core concepts of deep learning. 
These concepts are not independent but are connected as follows.

```
고차원 Raw Data  →  Embedding  →  Manifold 위의 구조 발견
                                          ↓
                                  Latent Space (저차원 표현)
                                          ↓
                              Epoch 반복으로 점점 정교해짐
```

## Embedding {#sec-embedding}

### Mathematical Definition

"When Object $X$ is embedded in $Y$, the embedding is given by 
the **injective** and **structure-preserving** function 
$f: X \to Y$."

In deep learning, it is specified as follows.

$$f_\theta: \mathbb{R}^D \to \mathbb{R}^d, \quad d \ll D$$

Two conditions are important.

**① Injective:**

$$x_1 \neq x_2 \implies f(x_1) \neq f(x_2)$$

Discriminability of information is preserved.

**② Structure-preserving:**

$$d_{\text{원공간}}(x_1, x_2) \approx d_{\text{임베딩}}(f(x_1), f(x_2))$$

Relationships in the original space are maintained in the embedding space as well. 
A representative example is the relationship preservation in Word2Vec.

$$\vec{\text{king}} - \vec{\text{man}} + \vec{\text{woman}} \approx \vec{\text{queen}}$$

### Types of embeddings

| Type | Input | Embedding Space | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Word Embedding | $\mathbb{R}^{|V|}$ (one-hot) | $\mathbb{R}^{300}$ | Word2Vec |
| Image Embedding | $\mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}$ | $\mathbb{R}^{512}$ | CNN feature |
| Neural Network | Input Layer | Each Hidden Layer | All Deep Learning |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Wireless Network Perspective

Compressing 
a high-dimensional channel matrix $\mathbf{H} \in \mathbb{C}^{N_r \times N_t}$ from CSI (Channel State Information) feedback into low-dimensional codewords 
is exactly what embedding is. Deep learning-based CSI compression, such as CsiNet, utilizes this principle.
:::

## Manifold {#sec-manifold}

### Mathematical Definition

"In mathematics, a $n$-dimensional manifold is 
a topological space in which the neighborhood of each point is **homeomorphic** to the $n$-dimensional Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^n$."

Simply put, it is a space that looks like a flat Euclidean space when viewed from a sufficiently close distance (locally).

The image of a **person standing on the Earth** on the slide conveys this intuition well. 
The Earth is a sphere existing in three-dimensional space, but its surface is two-dimensional. 
A location on the Earth's surface can be completely described using only two coordinates: latitude and longitude.

```
전체적으로(Globally):  구부러진 표면  (지구)
가까이서(Locally):     평평한 평면  (내 발 앞 땅)
```

### Manifold Hypothesis

This is one of the theoretical grounds on which deep learning works.

> Actual data is not evenly distributed in high-dimensional space, but,
> It is concentrated on a much lower-dimensional manifold.

Mathematically:

$$p_{\text{data}}(x) \text{ is concentrated near a manifold } \mathcal{M} \subset \mathbb{R}^D$$

$$\dim(\mathcal{M}) = d \ll D$$

Example: In a 28×28 = 784-dimensional image space, "natural handwriting images" 
exist only in a very small part (low-dimensional manifold) of this 784-dimensional space.

### Relationship with the Curse of Dimensions

The **Curse of Dimensionality** discussed in Goodfellow Ch. 5.11 
is overcome by the manifold hypothesis.

If the input dimension is $d$ and Z$v$ values are distinguished on each axis, the number of required regions 
increases exponentially with the dimension, reaching $O(v^d)$. Deep learning utilizes the Manifold Hypothesis 
to learn the fact that real data is concentrated on a low-dimensional manifold within a high-dimensional space.

The Autoencoder is a representative model for learning this manifold.

$$\text{Encoder: } \mathbb{R}^D \xrightarrow{f_\phi} \mathbb{R}^d, \quad
\text{Decoder: } \mathbb{R}^d \xrightarrow{g_\theta} \mathbb{R}^D$$

$$\min_{\phi, \theta} \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}} \|x - g_\theta(f_\phi(x))\|^2$$

## Latent Space {#sec-latent}

### Intuition

The puppeteer controls the entire complex movement of the puppet using only a few strings. 
What is visible (puppet movement, high dimension) is determined by what is invisible (string pulling, low dimension). 
The space of these invisible strings is precisely Latent Space.

### Mathematical Definition

$$\underbrace{x}_{\text{관측 가능}} = g(\underbrace{z}_{\text{잠재 변수}}) + \epsilon$$

$z \in \mathbb{R}^d$ are the hidden causes that generate data, and 
$g: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^D$ converts it into an observable form.

### Subspace vs Latent Space

| | Subspace | Latent Space |
|---|---|---|
| Origin | Linear Algebra | Probability Theory / Generative Models |
| Structure | Linear | Non-linearity allowed |
| Example | Principal Component Space of PCA | $z$ Space of VAE |

**PCA (Linear Subspace):**

$$z = W^\top x, \quad W \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times d} \text{ (직교 기저)}$$

**VAE (Non-linear Latent Space):**

$$q_\phi(z \mid x) \approx \mathcal{N}(\mu_\phi(x),\, \sigma^2_\phi(x))$$

Linear interpolation between two points $z_1$ and $z_2$ in a well-learned Latent Space 
generates meaningful intermediate data (continuity).

## Epoch {#sec-epoch}

### Definition

The **geological era stratigraphy** provides intuition. 
Just as each geological era is a complete unit of time with a clear beginning and end, 
the training epoch is also a complete unit that completely traverses the entire dataset once.

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| $N$ | Total number of training data |
| $b$ | Batch Size |
| **Iteration** | 1 parameter update |
| **Epoch** | $\lceil N/b \rceil$ Iteration = Cycle through the entire data once |

SGD Update Rule:

$$\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta \cdot \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}(\theta;\, B_t)$$

1 Epoch = Performing the above update $N/b$ times.

### Epoch Number and Training State

```
너무 적은 Epoch  →  Underfitting  (학습 부족)
적당한 Epoch    →  Generalization (목표 상태)
너무 많은 Epoch  →  Overfitting   (훈련 데이터 암기)
                          ↑
                   Early Stopping으로 방지
```

# Data Split: Train / Validation / Test {#sec-data-split}

## The role of the three sets

```
전체 데이터셋
  ├── Training Set    →  파라미터 θ 학습 (역전파)
  ├── Validation Set  →  하이퍼파라미터 λ 튜닝
  └── Test Set        →  최종 성능 단 한 번 측정
```

## Parameters vs Hyperparameters

| Classification | Definition | Example | Optimization Method |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Parameter** | Learn from data | Weights $W$, Bias $b$ | Gradient Descent |
| **Hyperparameter** | Control learning algorithm | Learning rate $\eta$, number of layers | **Explore with Validation Set** |

## Why is a Validation Set necessary?

Goodfellow states the key point in Chapter 5.3. 
If hyperparameters controlling the model's capacity are trained on the training data, 
the algorithm will always select the **maximum possible capacity**, which leads directly to overfitting.

$$\lambda^* = \arg\min_{\lambda \in \Lambda}\, \mathcal{L}_{\text{val}}\bigl(\theta^*(\lambda)\bigr)$$

::: {.callout-warning}
## Test Set No Contamination

During the hyperparameter tuning process through validation, repeatedly examining the test set 
effectively turns it into a second validation set. 
The final performance estimate becomes optimistically biased. 
"It's a crime!" — Lecture slides
:::

## Hyperparameter Automation: HPO

Hyperparameter tuning through the Validation Set is **fully automatable** and 
is actually automated in most modern ML pipelines.

| Method | Principle | Characteristics |
|---|---|---|
| **Grid Search** | Grid Search | Combination Explosion Problem |
| **Random Search** | Random Sampling | More Efficient Than Grid (Bergstra & Bengio, 2012) |
| **Bayesian Optimization** | Surrogate model + EI | Currently most widely used |
| **Gradient-based (DARTS)** | Implicit differentiation | Used for architecture exploration |

The Core of Bayesian Optimization:

$$\lambda_{\text{next}} = \arg\max_\lambda \text{EI}(\lambda), \quad
\text{EI}(\lambda) = \mathbb{E}\!\left[\max(0,\, f(\lambda) - f(\lambda^+))\right]$$

### K-Fold Cross-Validation

This is a method used when there is insufficient data.

$$E_{\text{CV}} = \frac{1}{K} \sum_{k=1}^K E_k$$

Divide the data into $K$ parts, using 1 part for validation and the remaining $K-1$ parts for training.

# Generalization and LLM {#sec-generalization}

## The Ultimate Goal of Machine Learning

> The ability to predict the correct output for unseen inputs by learning from training data

$$\text{목표: } E_{\text{train}} \approx E_{\text{test}}$$

who memorizes a little but reasons a lot is wiser than a student who memorizes everything but cannot reason ."

## Did LLM achieve generalization?

Conclusion: **Partially Yes, but the explanation is incomplete based on existing theories.**

### Conflict with Classical Theory

Generalization error of statistical learning theory bound:

$$E_{\text{test}} \leq E_{\text{train}} + O\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{\text{model complexity}}{N}}\right)$$

According to this, generalization should worsen as the model gets larger. 
However, GPT-4 (hundreds of billions of parameters) demonstrates excellent generalization. → **Double Descent Phenomenon**

### Limitations of LLM

| Limit | Description |
|---|---|
| Hallucination | Confidently generating incorrect information outside the training distribution |
| Distribution Shift | Unable to adapt to information after the training point |
| Reasoning Limitations | Systematic Failure in Complex Mathematical Reasoning |
| Shortcut Learning | Learning statistical patterns, not real concepts |

# ML vs Deep Learning {#sec-ml-vs-dl}

## Key Difference: Feature Engineering

| | Traditional ML | Deep Learning |
|---|---|---|
| Feature extraction | Human-designed | Automatic learning from data |
| Data Requirement | Relatively small amount is acceptable | Large amount of data required |
| Interpretability | Relatively High | Low (Black box) |
| High-dimensional data | Curse of dimensionality | Process effectively |

## Hierarchical Representation Learning in Deep Learning

According to Goodfellow Ch. 1, deep learning 
**constructs complex expressions from a combination of simple expressions**.

$$\text{Raw Data} \xrightarrow{\text{Layer 1: edges}}
\xrightarrow{\text{Layer 2: contours}}
\xrightarrow{\text{Layer 3: parts}}
\xrightarrow{\text{Layer 4: objects}} \text{Output}$$

::: {.callout-note}
## Representation Learning

Traditional ML designs features directly (hand-crafted features) by humans.

$$\text{Raw Data} \xrightarrow{\text{인간이 설계}} \text{벡터} \xrightarrow{\text{ML}} \text{출력}$$

Deep learning automatically learns this process from data.

$$\text{Raw Data} \xrightarrow{\text{Layer 1}} \xrightarrow{\text{Layer 2}} \cdots \xrightarrow{\text{Layer }L} \text{출력}$$
:::

## Why Traditional ML Fails: The Local Smoothness Assumption

According to Goodfellow Ch. 5.11, traditional ML 
relies on the **local smoothness assumption**. 
It estimates the output of a new input as the output of the nearest training point.

In high-dimensional space, this assumption is broken because there is not enough "near" training data (curse of dimensionality) 
. Deep learning overcomes this through **hierarchical representation learning**.

---

# Double Descent {#sec-double-descent}

## Classical Theory: Bias-Variance Tradeoff

Key formulas covered in Goodfellow Ch. 5.4:

$$\text{MSE}(\hat{\theta}) = \text{Bias}(\hat{\theta})^2 + \text{Var}(\hat{\theta})$$

Classical theory predicts that as model complexity (capacity) increases, bias decreases and variance increases, causing the test error to follow a U-shaped curve.

## Discovery of Double Descent

A phenomenon reported by Belkin et al. in 2019. When 
the model is expanded beyond the level where it can perfectly fit the training data (**Interpolation Threshold**), 
the Test Error **decreases again**.

```
Test Error
  │╲
  │ ╲                    ← Double Descent
  │  ╲      /╲          /
  │   ╲    /  ╲        /  (두 번째 감소)
  │    ╲  /    ╲______/
  │     \/
  │  Classical  Modern
  │  Optimal    Optimal
  └────┬──────────────── 모델 복잡도 N
       ↑
  Interpolation Threshold
  (Train Error → 0이 되는 지점)
```

## Three Regimes

| Regime | Condition | Attribute |
|---|---|---|
| ① Classical | $N_{\text{params}} \ll N_{\text{data}}$ | Bias Dominance, Traditional U-curve |
| ② Critical | $N_{\text{params}} \approx N_{\text{data}}$ | Test Error Max (Critical Section) |
| ③ Modern | $N_{\text{params}} \gg N_{\text{data}}$ | Train Error = 0, Test Error re-reduced |

## Reasons why it becomes generalized in Modern Regimes

### Implicit Regularization of SGD

SGD 
implicitly favors the **minimum norm solution** among the infinitely many solutions that satisfy the training data.

Set of solutions satisfying the training data in a linear model:

$$\{\theta : X\theta = y\}$$

tends to converge to the solution with the minimum of $\|\theta\|_2$ in this set, i.e., the **Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse solution**.

$$\theta^* = X^\top(XX^\top)^{-1}y$$

### Smooth Interpolation

With a much larger number of parameters, one can find a function that **smoothly** passes between training points. 
In the critical zone, the function must bend sharply, but 
in the Modern Regime, slack degrees of freedom lead to a smooth solution.

::: {.callout-note}
## Epoch-wise Double Descent

There is also a phenomenon that occurs the longer the same model is trained. 
Initially, it learns useful patterns (first-order descent), 
then memorizes noise (ascending), and 
after training long enough, it converges back to meaningful patterns (second-order descent). 
This is also the reason why **Early Stopping is not always the best option**.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Wireless Network Perspective

in the same context as the distribution shift problem 
in channel estimation, where performance drops sharply when a trained model goes out of the SNR range . 
Also, just as Compressed Sensing finds a sparse solution for an underdetermined system $M < N$ 
by minimizing the $\ell_1$ norm, 
SGD also induces implicit sparsity.
:::

# AGI and ASI {#sec-agi-asi}

## Three levels of AI

| Level | Definition | Current State |
|---|---|---|
| **ANI** (Narrow AI) | Excels only in specific tasks | ✅ Real (GPT-5, AlphaGo, etc.) |
| **AGI** (General AI) | Human-level General Intelligence | ❌ Not yet achieved |
| **ASI** (Super AI) | Transcends humans in every aspect | ❌ Theoretical concept |

```
지능 수준 축
────────────────────────────────────────────────►
      ANI                AGI               ASI
 [현재 우리 위치]      [미달성]           [이론적]
  특정 태스크만         인간 수준의        인간을 모든
  잘 하는 AI           범용 지능          면에서 초월
```

## Key Characteristics of AGI

**① Domain Transfer Learning:** Sharing representations between different distributions $p_1(x,y)$ and $p_2(x,y)$

$$f_{\text{AGI}}: \mathcal{X}_{\text{any}} \to \mathcal{Y}_{\text{any}}$$

**② Autonomous Goal Setting:** Define and pursue sub-goals on your own

**③ Few-shot / Zero-shot Generalization:** Performing unseen tasks with only a few examples

**④ Continuous Learning:** Acquiring new knowledge without catastrophic forgetting

**⑤ Metacognition:** Recognizing "what I don't know"

## ASI and Intelligence Explosion

The core scenario of ASI is **Recursive Self-improvement**.

```
AGI 달성
    ↓
AI가 자기 자신을 개선하는 코드 작성
    ↓
더 똑똑해진 AI가 또 자기 자신을 개선
    ↓  (기하급수적 폭발)
인간의 이해를 완전히 초월한 수준
```

If the rate of intelligence improvement is proportional to current intelligence:

$$\frac{dI}{dt} \propto I(t) \implies I(t) = I_0 e^{\alpha t}$$

This is called the **Intelligence Singularity** or **Technological Singularity**.

## Key Comparison of AGI vs ASI

| | AGI | ASI |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline | Human-level | Overwhelmingly transcendent |
| Self-improvement | Limited | Recursive self-improvement possible |
| Current Status | Unachieved | Purely Theoretical |
| Core Risk | Control Issues | Ontological Risk |

::: {.callout-important}
## Current LLM location

they cover the **widest range of tasks** 
among ANIs . 
As of 2026, no system has achieved true AGI.
:::

# Deep Learning Trends and Hardware

## Two key trends

1. **Dataset Scale is growing** (Dataset Scale ↑)
2. **Model is getting bigger** (Model Scale ↑)

This trend is the background behind the emergence of Foundation Models such as GPT-4, Sora, and Gen-4, and 
**GPU computing power** is essential for this.

## xPU types

| Type | Description |
|---|---|
| CPU | General Purpose Computation |
| GPU | Matrix operation specialized, core of deep learning training |
| TPU | Google's neural network training/inference specialized |
| NPU | Neural Network Inference Specialized (Mobile/Edge) |
| LPU | Language Inference Specialization, Fast Token Generation (Groq) |

---

# Key Summary

- Deep learning is a **machine learning methodology that uses deep neural networks**.
- The ultimate goal of ML is **Generalization** — the ability to predict on new data.
- Data is separated into Train / Validation / Test, and each role is strictly distinguished.
- Hyperparameter tuning can be **automated** through the Validation Set.
- Double Descent is a modern phenomenon that goes beyond classical Bias-Variance theory.
- Currently, all AI is ANI, and AGI/ASI has not yet been achieved.
